summary: This NIBIB science education page explains computed tomography (CT), describing how CT scanners produce cross-sectional and 3D images using rotating x-ray sources and digital detectors. It covers common clinical uses, contrast agents (iodine-based IV and barium-based oral), and radiation and kidney risks, especially for children and pregnant patients. It closes with three examples of NIBIB-funded CT projects on stroke imaging, metal artifact reduction, and AI for COVID-19.
one_line: NIBIB educational overview of computed tomography (CT), covering how scans work, clinical uses, contrast agents, risks, and NIBIB-funded CT research.
key_facts: CT is a computerized x-ray imaging procedure in which a narrow beam of x-rays is aimed at a patient and quickly rotated around the body to generate cross-sectional images called slices.
Unlike a conventional x-ray, a CT scanner uses a motorized x-ray source that rotates around the circular opening of a donut-shaped structure called a gantry.
CT scanners use special digital x-ray detectors located directly opposite the x-ray source instead of film.
The thickness of tissue represented in each CT image slice usually ranges from 1-10 millimeters, depending on the machine used.
Stacked CT slices can be digitally combined by the computer to generate a 3D image of the patient.
CT has become a useful screening tool for detecting possible tumors or lesions within the abdomen.
A CT scan is particularly useful when imaging complex bone fractures, severely eroded joints, or bone tumors since it usually produces more detail than a conventional x-ray.
For the circulatory system, an intravenous (IV) contrast agent based on iodine is injected into the bloodstream to help illuminate blood vessels.
Oral contrast agents, such as barium-based compounds, are used for imaging the digestive system, including the esophagus, stomach, and gastrointestinal (GI) tract.
CT scans use x-rays, and all x-rays produce ionizing radiation, a risk that increases with the number of exposures added up over the life of an individual.
IV contrast agents should not be administered to patients with abnormal kidney function since they may induce a further reduction of kidney function, which may sometimes become permanent.
Because children are more sensitive to ionizing radiation and have a longer life expectancy, they have a higher relative risk for developing cancer from such radiation compared with adults.
If imaging of the abdomen and pelvis is needed, doctors prefer exams that do not use radiation, such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or ultrasound.
NIBIB-funded researchers developed an image reconstruction technique to more efficiently triage patients who present with stroke symptoms, ruling out hemorrhage and finding the site of a blood clot.

NIBIB-funded researchers developed an algorithm to reduce metal artifacts in CT imaging without requiring knowledge of the implant material, with a potential application to prostate cancer radiation therapy planning for patients with hip prostheses.
NIBIB created the Medical Imaging and Data Resource Center (MIDRC) during the COVID-19 pandemic, which collected and analyzed thousands of CT images from patients with COVID-19.
